The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody expected much from Tuesdays. It occupied a former hardware store between a bakery and a shop that repaired shoes, and its sign was so modest that people sometimes mistook it for a notice about parking. MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS, it said. Beneath that, in smaller letters: Admission free. Please do not complete the exhibits. The curator, a woman named Ada, unlocked the door at nine, placed a bowl of peppermints beside the visitor book, and waited. For the first hour, nothing happened. She considered this an encouraging start.

The first exhibit was a blue sweater with one sleeve missing. It lay beneath glass, accompanied by a card explaining that its maker had learned to knit during a difficult winter, then stopped when spring arrived. There was no tragedy involved. The winter had simply ended, and with it the need to count stitches beside a radiator. Visitors were often disappointed by this explanation. They wanted a death, a departure, a letter discovered too late. Ada understood. She had once wanted stories to behave that way too, before she found herself inventing sad endings for perfectly happy strangers.

Across from the sweater stood a wooden boat small enough to carry under one arm. Its hull had been sanded smooth, but its mast remained a pencil mark on the plans beside it. A retired dentist had intended to sail it on the pond in the park. Instead, he had become interested in moths. He donated the boat with an apology and three photographs of a creature whose wings resembled fallen leaves. Ada displayed the photographs as well. She liked the boat, but the dentist had spoken so eagerly about the moths that leaving them out seemed unkind.

There were unfinished novels, of course. So many that Ada eventually gave them their own room. Some stopped halfway through a sentence. Others ended just before the detective named the murderer, as if the writer had developed a sudden loyalty to the suspect. One manuscript consisted entirely of chapter titles. Another contained four hundred pages describing a family breakfast during which nobody managed to pour the tea. Visitors could sit and read whatever they liked. Occasionally someone demanded to know how a story ended. Ada would point toward the bakery. “Perhaps they know,” she said. “They finish things every morning.”

Children understood the museum immediately. They examined a jigsaw puzzle with seventeen missing pieces and declared it a map of islands. They admired a half-painted wall because it looked like weather arriving. In front of an abandoned architectural model, a little girl observed that a staircase leading nowhere was still an excellent place to sit. Adults were less comfortable. They folded their arms. They read the labels twice. Some asked whether the exhibits were really art. Ada said she wasn’t sure, then asked whether they wanted a peppermint. It was difficult to sustain a formal objection while unwrapping a peppermint.

One afternoon, a man brought in a sealed envelope. He held it carefully by the edges, though it was neither old nor fragile. “It’s an apology,” he said. “I never sent it.” Ada asked whether he wanted it displayed. He looked around at the sweater, the boat, the room full of interrupted breakfasts. “I thought you might put it somewhere,” he said. She explained that donations did not have to remain forever. People occasionally reclaimed their work. The man nodded, but his hand stayed on the envelope for a long time after he had laid it on her desk.

Ada kept the letter in a drawer for three weeks. She did not open it. Then the man returned on a rainy Thursday and asked for it back. His coat dripped onto the floor while she searched beneath a bundle of unfinished crossword puzzles. “I’m going to send it,” he said. Ada handed him a tissue for his glasses. He stood near the door, reading the address through lenses he had only made wetter, and asked where he could buy a stamp. After he left, she wiped the floor and put the crossword puzzles back in the drawer.

Ada herself had an exhibit, though nobody knew it. In the storage room stood a cello in a black case. She had bought it at thirty-seven, believing that a sufficiently serious purchase might create a sufficiently serious person. For six months she practiced scales in an apartment with thin walls. Then her father became ill, and afterward there were arrangements, bills, rooms to empty. By the time she had an evening free, she could no longer remember where her fingers belonged. She brought the cello to the museum because the storage room was dry and her apartment was small.

Sometimes she took it out after closing. She never played a complete piece. Usually she drew the bow across an open string and listened until the sound faded beneath the refrigerator’s hum. The bakery next door prepared dough before dawn; the shoe repairer stayed late over stubborn heels. Ada liked hearing them through the walls as she struggled to tune. Once, the baker knocked to ask if she could play something for his daughter’s birthday. Ada explained how little she knew. He looked relieved. His daughter was learning the trumpet, he said, and might appreciate meeting another beginner.

By its second year, the museum had acquired a reputation. People arrived carrying canvases, business plans, language textbooks, and elaborate intentions involving exercise. Ada accepted only some of them. Space was limited, and the roof needed work. On quiet afternoons she sat by the entrance, repairing loose labels while visitors wandered through the rooms. Occasionally someone left without donating what they had brought. She would watch them cross toward the bakery, still carrying a sketchbook or a box of tools. Then she returned to her desk, where a visitor had once borrowed her pen and left its cap.
